sinks.name: dangerouslySetInnerHTML
sinks.severity_note: P2 as DOM/stored XSS; on SSR-rendered pages payload <script> executes at parse time (higher reliability than client-side insertion, where inline scripts are inert but event handlers fire).
sinks.explain: React escapes every value rendered in JSX by default. dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{__html: string}} is the deliberate opt-out: React assigns the string to the element's innerHTML verbatim, with zero sanitization. Any attacker influence over that string is XSS - the framework's protection ends exactly at this prop.
sinks.how_it_works: Client-side, React sets innerHTML on the DOM node: inline DOES execute at parse time, before React hydrates. Hydration does not re-sanitize; React trusts that server and client markup match, so a payload stored via SSR fires for every first-hit visitor. Also watch for the pattern dangerouslySetInnerHTML with a 'sanitizer' that is really a regex blacklist.
sinks.why_it_matters: This prop is React's single XSS hole and its name makes it trivial to grep in review. It is used for rich-text renderers, CMS content, and markdown output - precisely the data classes attackers control - and SSR turns it into a reliable stored/reflected XSS with script execution.

contexts.html-body: Client-side: event-handler vectors fire, inline <script> inert. SSR: <script> executes at parse time - prefer it for reliability.
contexts.attr: If the string is wrapped in markup that places it inside an attribute, break out with '">'.
contexts.js-string: If the value passes through a JS string first (e.g. JSON.parse of inline state), escape with '</script><svg onload=alert(1)>' in the SSR document.

sinks.waf_notes: SSR reflections are visible to server WAFs - mutate case (<ScRiPt>), use <svg onload> instead of <script>, or deliver via stored API fields and hash/postMessage sources that never hit the wire. React's escaping reputation means many codebases apply no secondary filter here.
sinks.eligibility: XSS through dangerouslySetInnerHTML is accepted on all major platforms; it is unambiguous framework-supported raw HTML. Note honestly whether the trigger is SSR (parse-time execution) or client-side (event-handler vectors only).
mitigations: Avoid dangerouslySetInnerHTML entirely; render structured data with components.
If unavoidable, sanitize with DOMPurify: dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{__html: DOMPurify.sanitize(data)}}.
Sanitize again server-side for SSR output and deploy a nonce-based CSP.

sinks.name: ng-bind-html
sinks.severity_note: P3 baseline because the AngularJS $sanitize pipeline (ngSanitize) strips most vectors; P2 when the bound value is pre-wrapped with $sce.trustAsHtml (or a sanitizer bypass applies to the exact AngularJS version). Angular 2+ [innerHTML] is sanitized by DomSanitizer - escalation needs bypassSecurityTrustHtml upstream.
sinks.explain: ng-bind-html renders a bound expression as HTML inside the element (AngularJS 1.x, with ngSanitize loaded, the value passes through $sanitize; without ngSanitize the app must trust the value via $sce). In Angular 2+ the equivalent is the [innerHTML] property binding, sanitized by DomSanitizer. Both are framework-sanctioned HTML renderers whose safety depends entirely on configuration and the sanitizer's strength for that version.
sinks.how_it_works: AngularJS $sanitize parses the HTML and whitelists tags/attributes - historically bypassed repeatedly (mutation-XSS via nested/namespace-confused markup against specific 1.x versions). If the code instead calls $sce.trustAsHtml(userValue) before binding, sanitization is skipped entirely and any markup executes. Angular 2+ DomSanitizer.sanitize(SecurityContext.HTML, ...) similarly whitelists; bypassSecurityTrustHtml(value) marks a string exempt. The review question is never 'is ng-bind-html present' but 'was the value trusted or does this version's sanitizer have a known bypass'.
sinks.why_it_matters: This is the standard rich-text renderer in Angular apps. The presence of trustAsHtml/bypassSecurityTrustHtml one hop upstream converts it into unconditional XSS, and legacy AngularJS apps pinned to old 1.x versions carry published sanitizer bypasses.

sinks.name: $sce.trustAsHtml
sinks.severity_note: P2 when applied to any attacker-influenced string - it disables the framework sanitizer by design; not exploitable on its own, it is the upstream switch that arms ng-bind-html/[innerHTML].
sinks.explain: $sce.trustAsHtml(value) (AngularJS) and DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml(value) (Angular 2+) wrap a string in a 'trusted' object the framework will render verbatim, skipping all sanitization. Reviewing these calls is reviewing the single decision that turns a sanitized binding into raw-HTML XSS.
sinks.how_it_works: AngularJS's Strict Contextual Escaping normally rejects untrusted strings in HTML contexts; trustAsHtml asserts 'I vouch for this'. The same holds for Angular's DomSanitizer: bypassSecurityTrustHtml produces a SafeHtml the renderer assigns without filtering. Typical vulnerable pattern: vm.body = $sce.trustAsHtml($routeParams.body) or a shared helper safeHtml(s) { return $sce.trustAsHtml(s); } applied indiscriminately. Once trusted, every markup vector (,
sinks.why_it_matters: These functions are grep-able red flags: any occurrence within reach of user data is a finding. They are common in legacy dashboards rendering 'admin-entered' HTML that later became editable by lower-privilege or external users.

sinks.name: {@html}
sinks.severity_note: P2 as DOM/stored XSS; Svelte applies zero sanitization to {@html}. Client-side insertion makes inline <script> inert but event handlers fire; SvelteKit SSR emits the string raw into the initial document where <script> executes at parse time.
sinks.explain: Svelte escapes {expression} output by default. The {@html expression} tag is the explicit raw-HTML directive: the string is inserted into the DOM as markup with no filtering. Any attacker influence over the expression is XSS.
sinks.how_it_works: At compile time {@html x} becomes an insertion of the raw string into the target node. During SSR (SvelteKit), the value is concatenated directly into the response HTML - <script>alert(document.domain)</script> in the value executes when the browser parses the initial page, before hydration. Client-side updates assign markup like innerHTML: event attributes (onerror, onload) fire, inline scripts do not. Grep for {@html in .svelte files; also watch components wrapping it (a 'RichText' component is often just {@html content} inside).
sinks.why_it_matters: {@html} is the only HTML-injection primitive in Svelte and is used for markdown/CMS rendering - attacker-controlled data classes. SvelteKit SSR makes the highest-reliability case (parse-time script execution) the default architecture.

sinks.explain: Handlebars escapes {{value}} interpolations by default. Triple-stash {{{value}}} disables escaping and emits the value as raw markup - the same effect as Handlebars.SafeString wrapping on the data side. Any user-controlled value rendered through either mechanism is XSS.
sinks.how_it_works: In server-side Node/Express apps, {{{body}}} with a request-derived value is textbook reflected or stored XSS delivered in the HTTP response - <script> executes at parse time, no DOM tricks needed. SafeString is the data-side twin: new Handlebars.SafeString(userValue) marks the value escape-exempt, so grep both {{{ and SafeString. Note the Ember variant (htmlSafe) follows the same rule.
sinks.why_it_matters: Triple-stash and SafeString are deliberate escaping bypasses that appear in email templates, PDF/HTML report generators, and CMS themes - server-rendered paths that many client-side-focused reviewers skip, yet they yield the most reliable XSS class (parse-time script execution).

sinks.severity_note: Severity is version-dependent: P2 on AngularJS >= 1.6 (sandbox removed - {{constructor.constructor('alert(1)')()}} executes directly) and on <= 1.1.5 (no sandbox); P3-P4 on 1.2-1.5 where a version-matched sandbox escape must be demonstrated; bare {{7*7}} arithmetic alone is often triaged as low/informational.
sinks.explain: Client-Side Template Injection (CSTI) in AngularJS: if an application reflects user input into the DOM inside an ng-app scope before AngularJS compiles it, an attacker can inject {{ }} expressions that AngularJS evaluates. Escalating from expression evaluation to JavaScript execution requires defeating (or the absence of) the AngularJS expression sandbox, which is entirely version-dependent.
sinks.how_it_works: AngularJS parses {{expression}} bindings during the $compile phase. Server-side reflection of parameters (e.g. ?name={{7*7}} rendered into the HTML inside an ng-app element) lets the attacker supply those bindings. The sandbox restricts access to window/constructor: AngularJS <= 1.1.5 had NO sandbox (direct {{constructor.constructor('alert(1)')()}}); 1.2.x-1.5.x shipped successive sandboxes, each publicly bypassed (e.g. the 1.2.x Gareth Heyes escape using Function.call chains via object accessors); 1.6.0 REMOVED the sandbox entirely, making expression injection equivalent to arbitrary JS again ({{constructor.constructor('alert(document.domain)')()}} works). Check the exact version with angular.version.full in the console before choosing the escape.
sinks.why_it_matters: CSTI is the framework-specific XSS class for the massive installed base of AngularJS 1.x apps (end-of-life since 2022, still widely deployed). Honest exploitation requires matching the escape to the running version - a strong report always states angular.version.full and shows the working chain for that version.
